# How modern AI models work {#sec-ch04}

You do not need to know how to build these models to use them well. But a few simple pictures help you understand why they behave the way they do. This chapter gives four such pictures, and then shows why asking an LLM like ChatGPT to make a decision is harder than it looks.

::: {.goals}
- How neural networks, embeddings and attention work, in simple words.
- Why big AI models are often too sure of themselves.
- Why it is hard to get a clean, reliable decision out of an LLM like ChatGPT.
:::

## Picture 1: a neural network is a team of small checkers

Think of a bank clerk who approves small loans with one simple habit: the higher the salary, the more likely the approval. That is exactly how the logistic regression from Chapter 2 works: points for each clue, added up. It can only think in one direction. More of something is always better, or always worse.

But some cases do not work like that. A card payment is suspicious if it is unusually *large*. It is also suspicious if it is unusually *small*: fraudsters often make ₹1 test payments to check whether a stolen card works. Normal payments sit in the middle. One simple rule that says "bigger is riskier" cannot catch both ends.

A **neural network** solves this by using a team of many small checkers, called **neurons**, arranged in layers:

- Each neuron in the first layer checks one simple thing: "Is the amount very large?" or "Is the amount very small?"
- The next layer combines their answers: "Suspicious if either one is true."
- With enough neurons and layers, the network can learn almost any pattern from examples.

A network with many layers is called **deep**, and this is where the name **deep learning** comes from. It learns the same way as in Chapter 2: guess, check the mistake, adjust, and repeat many times.

Neural networks are best at messy data, such as photos, voice and free text, where nobody could write the clues by hand. But when your data is already clean numbers, they add little. On the Kestrel alerts, a small neural network did no better than simple logistic regression.

::: {.keyidea}
**Big neural networks are for messy data like photos and text.** When your data is already clean numbers, such as a score or a count, a simple model works almost as well and is much easier to understand.
:::

## Picture 2: turning words into numbers

A computer can only work with numbers. So how does AI search find a document about "money not credited back" when a customer types "refund not received"?

Each piece of text is turned into a list of numbers called an **embedding**. The numbers are made so that texts with similar *meaning* get similar numbers, even when they use different words. It is like a library that keeps all the books on one topic on the same shelf: to find books about cricket, you go to the cricket shelf, whatever their titles say.

There is one limit. An embedding captures what a text is *about*, not the exact numbers inside it. To an embedding, "a payment of ₹50" and "a payment of ₹50,000" look almost the same, because both are about a payment. So when a decision depends on exact numbers, give those numbers to the model separately, not only inside the text.

## Picture 3: paying attention to the right words

"Payment failed, not fraud" and "Payment is fraud, not failed" use the same words but mean opposite things. When you read them, you notice the word "not" and flip the meaning.

Modern models do something similar, called **attention**. While reading each word, the model looks at the other words in the sentence and decides which ones change its meaning. Nobody teaches it about the word "not"; it learns this by itself from many examples. Many layers of attention stacked together make a **transformer**, the design behind ChatGPT and most modern AI.

## Picture 4: very large models, and why they sound so sure

Take a transformer and train it on a huge amount of text with one simple task: guess the next word. To guess well, it has to learn grammar, facts about the world and some reasoning. The result is a **large language model** (LLM) like ChatGPT. It is then improved further using feedback from people about which answers they like better.

This has a side effect. People usually prefer answers that *sound* confident. So the model learns to sound sure, like a salesman who never says "I don't know". On top of that, large models that are trained for a long time become over-sure anyway. The result is a model that says "I'm 99% sure" even when it is often wrong.

::: {.keyidea}
**Big models are often too sure of themselves.** After long training, they say "99% sure" even when they are often wrong. Always check their numbers on real cases before trusting them.
:::

## How an LLM writes, and why this is a problem for decisions

![The generation loop. The model reads everything so far, gives a chance to every possible next word, one gets picked and added, and the loop runs again.](/figures/ch10/loop.pdf){#fig-loop-06}

An LLM writes one small piece of text at a time, called a **token**: usually a word or part of a word. At each step it picks a likely next token, adds it, and repeats (@fig-loop-06). This causes three practical problems when you want a simple decision.

**Longer answers take more time and money.** Each token waits for the one before it. With typical figures, a one-word answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1 f1 >}} seconds, but a long step-by-step answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1500 int >}} seconds.

**The same question can get different answers.** The model picks each next word with a little randomness, like a person who answers slightly differently each time you ask. We sent forty borderline alerts to the model twenty times each, and {{< num ch10 n_split int >}} of them got different answers at different times.

**The answer is hidden inside text.** We can ask the LLM to reply like a filled-in form, for example `"verdict": "safe"`. (This form-like format is called **JSON**.) Even then, some replies come back broken: with friendly chatting around the form, cut off in the middle, or with extra items nobody asked for. Many LLMs have a setting that forces a proper form. But that only makes sure the form is filled in correctly, not that the answer is right. It is like a neatly written exam paper with the wrong answer.

![What came back when we asked an LLM to reply in a fixed form, for 4,000 alerts. Without the special setting, some replies had chatting around them, some were cut off, and some had extra items nobody asked for. With the setting on, the first two problems disappear, but the third does not.](/figures/ch11/json-failures.pdf){#fig-json-failures}

::: {.keyidea}
**A neatly formatted answer can still be wrong.** An LLM can return a perfect, clean "safe" for a real attack. Checking the format tells you the answer is readable, not that it is right.
:::

## Can we trust the LLM's "confidence"?

Suppose an LLM replies: `"verdict": "malicious", "confidence": 0.95`. Is it really 95% sure? Usually not:

- **The 0.95 is just text the model wrote**, like a student who writes "100% sure" next to every exam answer. In our example, the LLM used only {{< num ch11 n_distinct_stated int >}} different confidence values, almost always 0.9 or higher, whether the alert was a real attack or not. So the number tells you very little.
- **Some services also show how likely the model thought each word was.** This is a little better, but it is still too high, and it is about a *word*, not the answer: "malicious", "Malicious" and "likely malicious" all count separately.
- **A decision model like Jev is built differently.** It gives a number for the answer itself, which you can check on your own past cases, as in Chapter 2.

::: {.exercises}
1. A company says its classifier is "97% accurate" and gives a confidence with every answer. You plan to act automatically when the confidence is above 0.9. What would you check first?
:::
